          G6 LANDOWNERS LEGAL FUND, LLC’S REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS

       COMES NOW, G6 Landowners Legal Fund, LLC (“G6 Landowners”), and files this its

Reply to Exceptions to address issues and arguments raised by other parties regarding the Proposal

for Decision (“PFD”) issued by the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) in this matter. This Reply

to Exceptions addresses three topics: (1) the Applicants’ failure to establish the need for the Project

that is the subject of this proceeding; (2) the Applicants’ failure to hold adequate public meetings;

and (3) the ALJs’ correct conclusion that, if any route is chosen and approved for this Project,

Route 894 is the “best meets” route. G6 Landowners respectfully requests that the ALJs make no

substantive changes to their PFD and that the Commission adopt it as written.

       G6 Landowners would show as follows:

                 I. The Applicants Failed to Establish the Need for the Project

       The ALJs correctly concluded that the Applicants failed to establish the need for the

Project. The Commission may grant a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) only on
                                                1
 a showing by Applicants that the proposed transmission facility is necessary for the service,

accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. 1 The ALJs correctly determined that

circumstances have changed since the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”), on which the

Applicants’ assertion of need is based, was approved by the Commission in 2024. Of particular

importance, in June 2025, the Commission found: “Good cause exists due to the recent actual

experience in the ERCOT Region of previously forecasted loads coming into service at lower

megawatt level than initially claimed and the reasonableness of the level of adjustment made by

ERCOT to the Substantiated Load to account for this.” 2 The Commission’s decision resulted in a

27% reduction in the forecasted summer peak demand for 2031.3 Such a significant reduction

removes the foundation of the Applicants’ claim of need for the Project.

        The passage of SB 6 similarly changed the legal framework under which future loads are

forecasted. These changes directly impact the factual basis underlying the Applicants’ claim of

need, rendering it speculative at best.

        Further, the ALJs correctly determined that the record on which the Commission must base

its decision does not establish that Bell County East can supply power allegedly needed to flow

west into the Permian Basin.4 Of particular importance is ERCOT’s statement in its 2025 Regional

Transmission Plan:

            Central Texas faces the challenge of needing additional import capability. To
            meet the higher projected load demand in Central Texas, new flow patterns
            have emerged with imports to Central Texas coming from north of Austin
            and the Coast Weather Zone. Like the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP showed a
            need for additional import capacity along the pathway from north of Austin
            to Central Texas. 5

         According to ERCOT, Central Texas faces an import-capacity shortfall. Approval of the

Application would risk diverting capacity from that documented Central Texas need to serve a

Permian Basin forecast that the record shows to be overstated. Intervenors provided substantial

evidence demonstrating that the Permian Basin has sufficient resources to address reliability issues

locally rather than through the proposed import project.

        G6 Landowners specifically adopt and incorporate the following arguments, each

independently sufficient to sustain the ALJs’ denial recommendation: (1) the absence of any

partial-build study isolating the need for Import Path 2 as a standalone project, and the intervening

addition of approximately 39.467 GW of planned or announced gas-generation capacity in the

Permian Basin since the PBRP was adopted;6 (2) the absence of any determination that Central

Texas generation is sufficient to serve local load and simultaneously export westward at the

Project’s design capacity; 7 and (3) the Attorney General of Texas’s supplemental filing that House

Bill 5066 “makes no mention of extra high voltage 765-kilovolt lines” and that the Legislative

Budget Board’s fiscal note for that bill “included no additional anticipated costs to the state or

consumers.” 8

        Applicants are required to demonstrate need under PURA § 37.056(a) by a preponderance

of the evidence based on the circumstances that exist as of the date of its Application. Applicants

have instead relied on 2022 and 2024 studies and information and have failed to address the

significant changes in circumstances that render their evidence stale and unpersuasive. The ALJs

correctly evaluated and weighed the evidence in this proceeding. G6 Landowners respectfully

                        II. Applicants Failed to Hold Adequate Public Meetings

           The ALJs correctly concluded that Applicants did not comply with Rule 22.52(a)(4)’s

public-meeting notice requirements. Applicants expanded the study area and added roughly 400

miles of links after the June 2025 meetings. As a result, an additional 1,400 or so landowners

became affected by the Project after the Applicants’ public meetings were held. Applicants mailed

2,809 invitations to landowners for the June 2025 public meetings and mailed the March 26, 2026

application notices to over 4,200 parties – a 50% increase in affected landowners. Given the scope

of the changes and the number of newly affected landowners, the revised Project was in essence a

new Project for which no public meeting had been held.


           Applicants and Staff argue that the Commission’s decision in Docket No. 59315 resolves

this issue by holding that a single public meeting suffices regardless of subsequent route expansion.

However, Rule 22.52(a)(4) states, “The utility must hold at least one public meeting prior to the

filing of its licensing application if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail

notice of the application.” An interpretation of the rule that treats a single meeting as sufficient

under any circumstance, including the addition of 400 miles of new links and 1,400 new

landowners after the meeting was held, reads the word “at least” out of the rule entirely.


           The Texas Supreme Court has explained, “We presume that the Legislature chooses a

statute's language with care, including each word chosen for a purpose, while purposefully

omitting words not chosen.” 9 In the context of an agency’s interpretation of its own rule, “If the



9
    In re M.N., 262 S.W.3d 799, 802 (Tex.2008).
                                                  4
 Commission does not follow the clear, unambiguous language of its own regulation, we reverse

its action as arbitrary and capricious.” 10


           The Commission has established through its use of the phrase “at least” that there are

circumstances in which a single public meeting would be insufficient to meet the requirements of

Rule 22.52(a)(4). Surely the instance where an Applicant expanded the study area, added roughly

400 miles of links, and thereby added 1,400 or so affected landowners to the process would

constitute such circumstances. At a minimum, it is incumbent upon the Commission to explain

why it does not. Any other action would be arbitrary and capricious.


           G6 Landowners respectfully requests that the Commission adopt the ALJs’ PFD and deny

the Applicants’ Application for failure to comply with Rule 22.52(a)(4).


                           III. The ALJs Correctly Concluded that Route 894 is
                                 the “Best Meets” Route for this Proceeding

           The ALJs reviewed the extensive evidence that constitutes the record in this matter. As the

ALJs noted, 823 witnesses submitted written testimony, 1,398 exhibits were admitted into the

record, and 40 witnesses were cross-examined.11 The ALJs also made credibility determinations

that guided their decision-making. This role is critical to the outcome of this proceeding.

           Based on their review, the ALJs correctly concluded that Route 894 is the “best meets”

route for this proceeding. The Exceptions filed in this proceeding regarding routing do not raise

new substantive issues that have not already been considered and weighed by the ALJs.

           While other routes were proposed and considered by the ALJs, the record fully supports

the ALJs’ conclusion. G6 Landowners respectfully requests that the Commission, if necessary,


10
     Public Util. Comm'n of Tex. v. Gulf States Util. Co., 809 S.W.2d 201, 207 (Tex.1991).
11

 adopt this portion of the PFD and approve Route 894 as the required route to be used in the

implementation of the Project.

          Applicants identified nine routes of interest. Based on their review of the record, including

a consideration of witness testimony, the ALJs focused their review on four routes: Routes 894,

487, 392, and 296. The ALJs’ conclusion that Route 894 constitutes the “best meets” route is well

supported by the record in this proceeding.

          The ALJs did not find cost to be a distinguishing factor in selecting a route and found that

the lengths among the Focus Routes are also comparable.12 The ALJs found that Routes 487 and

894 achieved prudent avoidance more effectively than Route 296 and 392.13 The ALJs found that

Route 894 had less impact on park and recreational areas than Route 487, and performed favorably

on habitable structures, paralleling existing compatible ROW, crossing rangeland pasture, and

crossing riparian areas. The ALJs’ selection of Route 894 as the “best meets” route is supported

by the record and G6 Landowners respectfully requests that the Commission adopt the PFD in this

regard.

          This Reply to Exceptions focuses on arguments made in support of Route 296, as well as

Routes CCG, 891, and 572, which were not designated as “Focus Routes” by the ALJs.

          Reply to Route 296 Arguments

          Intervenors do not dispute that the Project’s proximity to Florence Elementary School is a

serious defect, and it is a proximity that parties on every side of this dispute treat as the most

serious community-values concern this record presents. But trading that concern for a different

 one is not a solution. Multiple intervenors have proposed, through Exceptions, workarounds when

the simplest and most complete solution has been available in the record from the outset: select

the route that never brings the Project near the school in the first place. As shown below, Route

894 is that route, and it achieves this result without sacrificing any of the advantages discussed

throughout this Reply.

         Save the Lampasas’s response illustrates the pattern. 14 Rather than dispute that the school’s

proximity is a serious defect, it argues the harm can simply be relocated, and that Route 296’s

proximity to Florence Elementary School should not be a disqualifying factor when link F34 can

be moved more than 1,000 feet away from the school. The record shows that Florence Elementary

School is located approximately 395 feet from the centerline of Link F34,15 and that Applicants

knew about the school nine months before filing the Application and never coordinated with the

school district.16 PUC Staff Engineer Mr. Poole agreed that had he been aware a route came within

such close proximity of an elementary school, it “would have affected [his prior] recommendation”

of Route 296.17 Tellingly, in its own Exceptions to the PFD, PUC Staff did not renew its advocacy

for Route 296.

         To allow the Applicant, post-hearing, to move a link the significant distance of over 600

feet defeats the purpose of the pre-application, application, and hearing processes. The

Commission’s task is to weigh the routes as filed and as supported by the evidentiary record

developed at hearing, not to select a route based on a non-litigated modification whose feasibility,

cost, and effect on other landowners were never tested through discovery or cross-examination.

 The Applicant made its decision as to the appropriate placement of link F34 and, for purposes of

this proceeding, it is bound by that decision. Further, Route 296 utilizes link F6, which also impacts

Florence Elementary School and would not be addressed by any proposed adjustment to Link F34

alone. In addition, as discussed in further detail below, Route 296 underperforms Route 894 on

other criteria, further showing that the selection of Route 296 as the “best meets” route is not

supported by the record and would simply be inappropriate.

           Intervenors promoting the selection of Route 296 have attempted to dismiss habitable-

structure count that serves as a basis for the Commission’s consideration of prudent avoidance.

Route 296 has 20 more habitable structures than Route 894, a staggering 24% differential. The

ALJs distinguished the performance of Route 894 over Route 296 on the basis of prudent

avoidance and specifically discussed the presence of Florence Elementary School and the habitable

structure differential as a basis for that decision.18 The ALJs particularly noted that Link G6, used

by Route 296, “has 16 habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline, tying for tenth highest,

making it one of the more residentially dense links.”19 The ALJs correctly differentiated Routes

894 and 296 on the basis of the prudent avoidance criterion. The ALJs’ conclusion in this regard

is fully supported by the record.

           Other Intervenors have promoted the use of link J31 for its paralleling of an existing

pipeline corridor. Link J31 crosses confirmed Golden-Cheeked Warbler-occupied habitat per

Applicants' witness Phillips, and parallels a petroleum pipeline, raising its own unaddressed

 cathodic-protection/stray-current engineering concern.20 These issues have been considered by the

ALJs and support their conclusion not to recommend Route 296 as a “best meets” route.

          Intervenors promoting the selection of Route 296 have raised viewshed considerations. 21

The Commission's EA methodology measures foreground visual zone impact at 0.5 miles, and

Route 894 has zero miles of ROW within that zone, no parks within 1,000 feet of its centerline,

and crosses no parks or recreational areas, which is the identical result reached for Route 296 on

each of the same measures. Beyond the metric established by the Commission’s EA methodology,

the argument for preferring Route 296 rests on a visual preference presented by a proportionally

small number of intervenors for greater distance from the parks, unmoored from any Commission-

adopted standard. Accepting that preference would require the Commission to trade Route 894’s

measurable advantages in habitable structures, cultural resources, and prudent avoidance for a

position advanced by a subset of parties that finds no support in the Commission’s own established

metric.

          Intervenor Carpenter advocates on behalf of his ranch – Greenwood Creek Ranch 22 – but

fails to acknowledge the Project’s bisection of property is not unique to the Carpenters. Mr. Poole

agreed that the G6 Link crossing the Taylor-Rose Ranch adds approximately 7,000 linear feet of

historic property crossed by the route, a fact not reflected anywhere in the Applicants’ cultural

resources data for the G6 Link. If selected, Route 891 would bisect the properties of a staggering

16 landowners on the G6 Link alone,23 including the Rose Family’s heritage ranch.24

        For the foregoing reasons, the ALJs correctly concluded that Route 296 should be rejected

from consideration as a “best meets” route. No changes should be made to the PFD in this regard.

        Reply to Route CCG Arguments

        The ALJs concluded that Route CCG did not “present a clear advantage over the Focus

Routes overall.” Route CCG’s advocate, Intervenor Cherokee Creek Partners (“CCP”), advocates

for an "appropriate weighing of the routing factors.”26 Such an analysis is exactly what the ALJs

performed, and, independently, exactly what Mr. Hopkins’ disclosed route-ranking model

ranking. CCP’s own chart, included on pages 7-9 of its Exceptions, demonstrates as much.

        Route 894 dominates Route CCG on 14 separate metrics, including:

                 (1) total transmission line cost;
                 (2) length;
                 (3) habitable structures;
                 (4) length through commercial/industrial areas;
                 (5) length across rangeland pasture;

        Route CCG’s total project cost increase of $73.7 million compared to Route 894 is enough

to disqualify Route CCG from consideration. The significant excess cost is not offset by a

corresponding benefit. As Mr. Hopkins testified, “Route CCG’s total project cost is $2.150 billion

- $74 million more than Route 894… Route CCG has 105 habitable structures – 24% more than

Route 894… Route CCG has 346 stream crossings – 19% more than Route 894’s 291.” 28 Route

CCG’s impact on 20 additional habitable structures and 21 additional Barn/Garage/Shed (“BGS”)

structures, as compared to Route 894, further demonstrates the inferiority of Route CCG.

         Reply to Route 891 Arguments

        While Route 891 was presented at the hearing as a “route of interest,” it was not identified

as a “Focus Route” by the ALJs, and for good reason. Route 891 was not even identified by the

Applicants as one of the best 122 routes to be included in its Application. The Exceptions

submitted by the main advocate for Route 891, the Sneeds, do not change the analysis: in a statute-

driven comparison, Route 891 remains inferior to Route 894.

        The Sneeds have proposed an “active opposition” recalculation of habitable structure

counts to include only those structures owned by those who actively intervened in this proceeding.

The Sneeds propose inventing a metric with no basis in statute or Commission rule. The proposal

should be summarily rejected.

        Measured by the same EA-based count applied to every other route in this record, Route

891 impacts significantly more habitable structures than Route 894, affecting 108 compared to 85,

or 23 more structures, at a notable 27% increase.37 The principal benefit advanced by the Sneeds

for Route 891 is avoiding impacts to their property. While unfortunate, the Project’s bisection of

property is not unique to the Sneeds. As discussed above, if selected, Route 891 would bisect 16

landowners on the G6 Link alone,38 including the Rose Family’s heritage ranch.39

        The Sneeds further contend that Route 891 parallels property boundaries more effectively

than Route 894 (44% compared to 41%), but this point does not withstand scrutiny. The very metric

on which the Sneeds rely, paralleling of apparent property boundaries, as opposed to paralleling of

existing electric transmission lines, pipelines, railroads, or public roads and highways, is the

identical metric that numerous other intervenors in this docket, including parties aligned with the

        The ALJs correctly determined that Route 891 does not “present a clear advantage over the

        Reply to Route 572 Arguments

        Intervenor Carpenter proposes Route 572, or a hybrid of Routes 572 and 296, as a fallback

if the Commission declines to select Route 296 because of its proximity to Florence Elementary

School, which is a serious routing defect as discussed above. But Route 572 does not eliminate the

harm Florence Elementary’s proximity to this project represents; it relocates that harm onto a

greater number of habitable structures and an already-compromised river crossing.

        This is seen in the fact that Route 572 fares no better than Route 296 under the record

evidence, including Mr. Hopkins’ disclosed route-ranking model, which ranks Route 572 38th of

123 evaluated routes. As Mr. Hopkins testified, “Route 572 is the weakest of the three Brewer

recommendations. It ranks #38 in my analysis, 37 spots below Route 894. Route 572 has 107

habitable structures, which is 26% more than Route 894's total of 85.” 41

        Route 572 also crosses the Colorado River at Link J31, which is the same crossing this

record shows to traverse confirmed Golden-Cheeked Warbler-occupied habitat, as Applicants'

witness Phillips confirmed, and to parallel a petroleum pipeline raising an unaddressed cathodic-



 PFD, at 105.

 protection and stray-current engineering concern.42 Route 572 therefore inherits the same

environmental and engineering defects that independently disqualify Route 296 and Route CCG

from consideration.

         Because Routes 572 and 894 are identical from Bell County through Link G13, avoiding

Link F34 is the sole benefit Route 572 offers, but it is purchased at the cost of a confirmed

environmental defect at Link J31 and a 26% greater impact on habitable structures. Route 894

achieves what Route 572 cannot: it avoids Florence Elementary School and imposes fewer

habitable-structure impacts than every alternative proposed in this proceeding. The Commission

should reject Route 572 for the same reasons it should reject Routes 296 and CCG: each asks the

Commission to accept a materially inferior route in exchange for avoiding a single defect that

Route 894 avoids without any tradeoff at all.

         The ALJs rejected consideration of Route 572 as a “focus route.” 43 Compared to Route

894, Route 572 costs more; is longer; has a lower percentage of paralleling of compatible right-of-

pasture; impacts more potential wetlands; requires 45 more stream crossings; and impacts more

lakes or ponds and more known rare/unique plant locations within right-of-way. Route 572 also

performs more poorly in the following categories: Number of recorded cultural resources within

1,000 feet of the route centerline; Length of route across areas of high archeological/historical site

                         II. Applicants Failed to Hold Adequate Public Meetings

          The ALJs correctly concluded that Applicants did not comply with Rule 22.52(a)(4)'s

public-meeting notice requirements. Applicants expanded the study area and added roughly 400

miles of links after the June 2025 meetings. As a result, an additional 1,400 or so landowners

became affected by the Project after the Applicants' public meetings were held. Applicants mailed

2,809 invitations to landowners for the June 2025 public meetings and mailed the March 26,2026

application notices to over 4,200 parties - a 50% increase in affected landowners. Given the scope

of the changes and the number ofnewly affected landowners, the revised Project was in essence a

new Project for which no public meeting had been held.


          Applicants and Staff argue that the Commission's decision in Docket No. 59315 resolves

this issue by holding that a single public meeting suffices regardless of subsequent route expansion.

However, Rule 22 . 52 ( a )( 4 ) states , " The utility must hold at least one public meeting prior to the

filing of its licensing application if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail

notice of the application." An interpretation of the rule that treats a single meeting as sufficient

under any circumstance, including the addition of 400 miles of new links and 1,400 new

landowners after the meeting was held, reads the word "at /easf ' out of the rule entirely.


          The Texas Supreme Court has explained, "We presume that the Legislature chooses a

statute's language with care, including each word chosen for a purpose, while purposefully

omitting words not chosen."9 In the context of an agency' s interpretation of its own rule, "If the




9 In re M. N„ 161 S . W. 3d 799 , 802 (Tex . 2008 ).

 Commission does not follow the clear, unambiguous language of its own regulation, we reverse

its action as arbitrary and Capricious."10


          The Commission has established through its use of the phrase "at leasf' that there are

circumstances in which a single public meeting would be insufficient to meet the requirements of

Rule 22.52(a)(4). Surely the instance where an Applicant expanded the study area, added roughly

400 miles of links, and thereby added 1,400 or so affected landowners to the process would

constitute such circumstances. At a minimum, it is incumbent upon the Commission to explain

why it does not. Any other action would be arbitrary and capricious.

the Applicants' Application for failure to comply with Rule 22.52(a)(4).
